claim: Porphyrias are disorders of heme metabolism frequently characterized by extreme photosensitivity.
source: Porphyrias are disorders of heme metabolism frequently characterized by extreme photosensitivity.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about porphyrias that draws from established medical knowledge about these disorders.

claim: Extreme photosensitivity in porphyrias results from accumulation of porphyrins, tetrapyrrole intermediates in heme biosynthesis that generate reactive oxygen species when exposed to light, in the skin of affected individuals.
source: This symptom results from accumulation of porphyrins, tetrapyrrole intermediates in heme biosynthesis that generate reactive oxygen species when exposed to light, in the skin of affected individuals.
evidence: This statement explains the mechanism of photosensitivity in porphyrias based on established scientific understanding.

claim: The planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea generates porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells under physiological conditions.
source: Here we report that in addition to producing an ommochrome body pigment, the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea generates porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells under physiological conditions
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including fluorescence analysis, absorption spectra, and gene expression patterns shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: S. mediterranea produces an ommochrome body pigment in addition to porphyrins.
source: Here we report that in addition to producing an ommochrome body pigment, the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea generates porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells under physiological conditions
evidence: This is supported by absorption spectra showing characteristic ommochrome peaks and RNAi experiments affecting ommochrome biosynthesis genes (Figure 2).

claim: Porphyrin production in S. mediterranea leads to pigment cell loss when animals are exposed to intense visible light.
source: the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea generates porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells under physiological conditions, and that this leads to pigment cell loss when animals are exposed to intense visible light.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing light-induced depigmentation, pigment cell loss visualized by in situ hybridization, and rescue of photosensitivity by PBGD-1 knockdown (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: Porphyrin biosynthesis and light-induced depigmentation in S. mediterranea are enhanced by starvation.
source: Remarkably, porphyrin biosynthesis and light-induced depigmentation are enhanced by starvation
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased ALAS expression with starvation, increased porphyrin fluorescence in starved D. japonica, and accelerated depigmentation in starved animals (Figure 7).

claim: Decreased nutrient intake precipitates acute manifestations in some porphyrias.
source: recapitulating a common feature of some porphyrias – decreased nutrient intake precipitates an acute manifestation of the disease.
evidence: This is a known clinical feature of acute porphyrias referenced from established medical literature.

claim: Planarians are an experimentally tractable animal model for research into the pathophysiology of acute porphyrias.
source: Our results establish planarians as an experimentally tractable animal model for research into the pathophysiology of acute porphyrias
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing parallels between planarian porphyrin metabolism and acute porphyrias.

claim: Heme plays a key role in proteins with diverse cellular functions, including oxygen binding, electron transfer, protection from oxidative stress, and generation of second messengers.
source: The prosthetic group heme plays a key role in proteins (hemoproteins) with diverse cellular functions, including oxygen binding (hemoglobin and myoglobin), electron transfer (cytochromes), protection from oxidative stress (catalases and peroxidases), and generation of second messengers (nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase) (Ponka, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ponka, 1999.

claim: Heme is essential for viability in all 3 domains of life, with few exceptions.
source: With few exceptions (Kořený et al., 2012), it is essential for viability in all 3 domains of life.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kořený et al., 2012.

claim: Heme is composed of a heterocyclic tetrapyrrole called a porphyrin coordinated to a central iron atom.
source: Heme is composed of a heterocyclic tetrapyrrole called a porphyrin coordinated to a central iron atom
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Heme is usually synthesized from the precursor 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) through a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
source: Although naturally occurring auxotrophs have been reported (Rao et al., 2005; Gruss et al., 2012), heme is usually synthesized from the precursor 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) through a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
evidence: This statement describes the heme biosynthesis pathway and is supported by citations.

claim: In non-photosynthetic eukaryotes, ALA is produced in the mitochondria via condensation of glycine and succinyl CoA by ALA synthase (ALAS).
source: In non-photosynthetic eukaryotes, ALA is produced in the mitochondria via condensation of glycine and succinyl CoA by ALA synthase (ALAS).
evidence: This describes a specific biochemical reaction in the heme biosynthesis pathway based on established knowledge.

claim: ALA synthesis by ALAS is the first and typically rate-limiting step in the heme biosynthesis pathway.
source: This is the first and typically rate-limiting step in the heme biosynthesis pathway, which proceeds in the cytoplasm before returning to the mitochondria (Layer et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Layer et al., 2010.

claim: The enzymes catalyzing the 8 reactions in the heme biosynthesis pathway are tightly regulated by ubiquitous and tissue-specific mechanisms.
source: Like ALAS, the enzymes catalyzing the 7 remaining reactions in the pathway are tightly regulated by ubiquitous and tissue-specific mechanisms (Ponka, 1997; Balwani and Desnick, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ponka, 1997 and Balwani and Desnick, 2012.

claim: Inherited, loss-of-function mutations in any of the heme biosynthesis enzymes downstream of ALAS (or gain-of-function mutations in ALAS) cause porphyrias.
source: Inherited, loss-of-function mutations in any of the heme biosynthesis enzymes downstream of ALAS (or gain-of-function mutations in ALAS) cause a group of diseases collectively referred to as porphyrias.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic basis of porphyrias based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Porphyrias are marked by characteristic clinical features including neurovisceral symptoms, skin lesions, or both.
source: These conditions are marked by characteristic clinical features – neurovisceral symptoms, skin lesions, or both (Karim et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Karim et al., 2015.

claim: The primary etiology of porphyria symptoms entails a buildup of pathway intermediates due to the bottleneck effect created by underlying mutations.
source: While potentially attributable at least in part to heme deficiency, the primary etiology of these symptoms entails a buildup of pathway intermediates due to the bottleneck effect created by underlying mutations.
evidence: This is an explanation of disease mechanism based on established understanding of porphyrias.

claim: ALA, and possibly also its pyrrole derivative porphobilinogen (PBG), is neurotoxic.
source: ALA, and possibly also its pyrrole derivative porphobilinogen (PBG), is neurotoxic (Pierach and Edwards, 1978; Adhikari et al., 2006; Felitsyn et al., 2008; Bissell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Porphyrins cause cutaneous abnormalities by virtue of their photosensitizing properties.
source: Porphyrins cause cutaneous abnormalities by virtue of their photosensitizing properties.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on established knowledge of porphyrin photochemistry.

claim: Porphyrins are generated primarily in the liver or bone marrow, the major sites of heme biosynthesis.
source: Though generated primarily in the liver or bone marrow, the major sites of heme biosynthesis, they are eventually deposited in other tissues including the dermis.
evidence: This describes the tissue distribution of heme biosynthesis based on established knowledge.

claim: Porphyrins readily absorb light to enter an excited triplet state that reacts with oxygen to produce singlet oxygen.
source: There, they readily absorb light to enter an excited triplet state that reacts with oxygen to produce singlet oxygen.
evidence: This describes the photochemical mechanism of porphyrin-mediated photosensitization based on established knowledge.

claim: Singlet oxygen produced by porphyrins results in oxidative damage, such as lipid peroxidation and DNA damage, that can ultimately lead to cell death.
source: This in turn results in oxidative damage, such as lipid peroxidation and DNA damage, that can ultimately lead to cell death (Poh-Fitzpatrick, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Poh-Fitzpatrick, 1986.

claim: Sunlight, or even bright indoor light, quickly damages exposed skin in many porphyria patients.
source: Thus, sunlight, or even bright indoor light, quickly damages exposed skin in many porphyria patients.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about porphyria patients based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Porphyrin-mediated phototoxicity manifests clinically as edema, blistering skin lesions, and in extreme cases, disfiguring scarring and/or tissue loss.
source: Clinically, porphyrin-mediated phototoxicity manifests as edema, blistering skin lesions, and in extreme cases, disfiguring scarring and/or tissue loss (Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Karim et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Balwani and Desnick, 2012 and Karim et al., 2015.

claim: Acute porphyrias present with sudden and potentially life-threatening attacks characterized by severe abdominal pain and neurological symptoms ranging from anxiety and confusion to seizures or paralysis.
source: A subset of porphyrias classified as 'acute' present with sudden and potentially life-threatening attacks characterized by severe abdominal pain and neurological symptoms ranging from anxiety and confusion to seizures or paralysis (Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Karim et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Balwani and Desnick, 2012 and Karim et al., 2015.

claim: Acute porphyria episodes can last for weeks.
source: These episodes, which can last for weeks, are triggered by drugs (e.g., barbiturates), hormonal changes, dieting/fasting, and other factors that induce hepatic ALAS expression or activity.
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of acute porphyrias based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Acute porphyria episodes are triggered by drugs (e.g., barbiturates), hormonal changes, dieting/fasting, and other factors that induce hepatic ALAS expression or activity.
source: These episodes, which can last for weeks, are triggered by drugs (e.g., barbiturates), hormonal changes, dieting/fasting, and other factors that induce hepatic ALAS expression or activity.
evidence: This describes known triggers of acute porphyria attacks based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Acute porphyria episodes are treated with therapies that effect ALAS downregulation.
source: Accordingly, they are treated with therapies that effect ALAS downregulation.
evidence: This describes the therapeutic approach to acute porphyrias based on established medical practice.

claim: Carbohydrate loading reduces ALAS levels via insulin signaling and an antagonistic effect on its transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α.
source: Carbohydrate loading reduces ALAS levels via insulin signaling and an antagonistic effect on its transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1α) (Scassa et al., 2004; Handschin et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Scassa et al., 2004 and Handschin et al., 2005.

claim: Carbohydrate loading is sometimes effective in ameliorating mild acute porphyria attacks.
source: This is sometimes effective in ameliorating mild attacks.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about treatment efficacy based on established medical practice.

claim: More severe acute porphyria cases are treated with intravenous heme.
source: More severe cases are treated with intravenous heme, which downregulates ALAS expression through a feedback inhibition mechanism (Bonkowsky et al., 1971; Ponka, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bonkowsky et al., 1971 and Ponka, 1997.

claim: Intravenous heme downregulates ALAS expression through a feedback inhibition mechanism.
source: More severe cases are treated with intravenous heme, which downregulates ALAS expression through a feedback inhibition mechanism (Bonkowsky et al., 1971; Ponka, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bonkowsky et al., 1971 and Ponka, 1997.

claim: A small interfering RNA therapy targeting ALAS decreased plasma ALA and PBG levels in a mouse model of acute porphyria.
source: A small interfering RNA therapy targeting ALAS decreased plasma ALA and PBG levels in a mouse model of acute porphyria (Yasuda et al., 2014), and entered clinical trials in 2015 (Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, 2016, NCT02452372).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yasuda et al., 2014.

claim: A small interfering RNA therapy targeting ALAS entered clinical trials in 2015.
source: A small interfering RNA therapy targeting ALAS decreased plasma ALA and PBG levels in a mouse model of acute porphyria (Yasuda et al., 2014), and entered clinical trials in 2015 (Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, 2016, NCT02452372).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, 2016, NCT02452372.

claim: Porphyrins accumulate under physiological circumstances in some organisms.
source: Given their toxic effects in porphyrias, it is interesting to note that porphyrins accumulate under physiological circumstances in some organisms.
evidence: This is a general observation supported by the examples that follow in the text.

claim: Porphyrins or their derivatives are pigments in the wing feathers of owls.
source: Porphyrins or their derivatives are pigments in the wing feathers of owls (With, 1978; Weidensaul, 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to With, 1978 and Weidensaul, 2011.

claim: Porphyrins or their derivatives are pigments in the brilliant crimson flight feathers of turacos.
source: the brilliant crimson flight feathers of turacos (With, 1957)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to With, 1957.

claim: Porphyrins or their derivatives are pigments in numerous invertebrate lineages including earthworms, molluscs, and deep-sea medusae.
source: and numerous invertebrate lineages including earthworms, molluscs, and deep-sea medusae (Kennedy, 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kennedy, 1975.

claim: High levels of porphyrins are present in the rodent Harderian gland.
source: It has been known for close to a century that high levels of porphyrins are present in the rodent Harderian gland (Derrien and Turchini, 1924)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Derrien and Turchini, 1924.

claim: High levels of porphyrins are present in multiple tissues of the fox squirrel Sciurus niger.
source: as well as in multiple tissues of the fox squirrel Sciurus niger (Turner, 1937)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Turner, 1937.

claim: Porphyrins are produced by bacteria such as Propionibacterium acnes, a commensal skin microbe that contributes to the pathogenesis of acne.
source: Porphyrins are also produced by bacteria such as Propionibacterium acnes, a commensal skin microbe that contributes to the pathogenesis of acne (Lee et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 1978.

claim: Previous biochemical studies documented physiological porphyrin biosynthesis in the planarian Girardia (formerly Dugesia) dorotocephala.
source: Here we extend previous biochemical studies documenting physiological porphyrin biosynthesis in the planarian Girardia (formerly Dugesia) dorotocephala (MacRae, 1956; 1959; 1961; 1963)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to MacRae, 1956; 1959; 1961; 1963.

claim: S. mediterranea uses the first 3 enzymes in the heme biosynthesis pathway to generate porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells.
source: by showing the related planarian species Schmidtea mediterranea uses the first 3 enzymes in the heme biosynthesis pathway to generate porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by gene expression data (Figure 4B) and RNAi experiments (Figure 4F).

claim: Sunlight exposure causes depigmentation of both regenerating and intact planarians.
source: This line of research originated with a serendipitous discovery in an undergraduate, general education course – sunlight exposure causes depigmentation of both regenerating and intact planarians (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by observational data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Infrared (IR) and ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation were neither necessary nor sufficient to induce depigmentation in S. mediterranea under tested conditions.
source: Infrared (IR) and ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation were neither necessary nor sufficient to induce depigmentation under conditions we tested in follow-up experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intense visible light is sufficient to reproduce the depigmentation response in S. mediterranea.
source: In contrast, we were able to reproduce this response with intense visible light (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A, 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 51% of light-exposed S. mediterranea animals developed one or more small tissue lesions on their dorsal surface.
source: Just over half of light-exposed animals (51%; n = 864 analyzed in 18 independent experiments) developed one or more small tissue lesions on their dorsal surface
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental observations.

claim: 4% of light-exposed S. mediterranea animals lysed.
source: 4% lysed.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental observations.

claim: Depigmented S. mediterranea animals exhibit normal movement.
source: Apart from these defects and their lack of bodily pigmentation, depigmented animals were indistinguishable from controls, exhibiting normal movement (Video 1)
evidence: This is supported by observational data shown in Video 1.

claim: Depigmented S. mediterranea animals exhibit normal touch-responsiveness.
source: touch-responsiveness (Video 2)
evidence: This is supported by observational data shown in Video 2.

claim: Depigmented S. mediterranea animals exhibit normal feeding behavior.
source: feeding behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Depigmented S. mediterranea animals exhibit normal regenerative ability.
source: and regenerative ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Depigmented S. mediterranea animals repigmented when light exposure stopped.
source: Depigmented animals repigmented when light exposure stopped (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E.

claim: Light-induced depigmentation in S. mediterranea was non-uniform.
source: Two observations indicated light-induced depigmentation was not a simple photobleaching effect. First, depigmentation was non-uniform (Figure 1C–E)
evidence: This is supported by observational data shown in Figures 1C–E.

claim: S. mediterranea animals subjected to a 24-hr pulse of light exposure continued to depigment for several days after light exposure stopped.
source: Second, animals subjected to a 24-hr pulse of light exposure continued to depigment for several days after light exposure stopped (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Prolonged exposure to intense visible light is sufficient to induce a reversible depigmentation response in S. mediterranea.
source: We conclude that prolonged exposure to intense visible light is sufficient to induce a reversible depigmentation response in S. mediterranea.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: The planarian Dugesia ryukyuensis produces a brown body pigment previously classified as an ommochrome on the basis of its absorption spectrum.
source: The planarian Dugesia ryukyuensis, which also exhibits a brown color, produces a body pigment previously classified as an ommochrome on the basis of its absorption spectrum (Hase et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hase et al., 2006.

claim: A S. mediterranea body pigment co-purifying with RNA exhibited characteristic local absorption maxima near 367 and 463 nm.
source: We found that a S. mediterranea body pigment co-purifying with RNA (Materials and methods), like the D. ryukyuensis ommochrome, exhibited characteristic, local absorption maxima near 367 and 463 nm
evidence: This is supported by absorption spectra data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mock pigment purification from depigmented S. mediterranea animals resulted in minimal absorbance.
source: a mock pigment purification from depigmented animals resulted in minimal absorbance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by absorption spectra data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ommochromes are tryptophan-derived pigments produced in the eyes of many insect species, including Drosophila.
source: Ommochromes are tryptophan-derived pigments produced in the eyes of many insect species, including Drosophila.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about ommochrome biosynthesis.

claim: Ommochrome biosynthesis involves an evolutionarily conserved pathway consisting of 4 steps.
source: Their biosynthesis involves an evolutionarily conserved pathway consisting of 4 steps (Ryall and Howells, 1974).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ryall and Howells, 1974.

claim: A total of 7 S. mediterranea genes corresponding to the first 3 steps in the ommochrome biosynthesis pathway were identified.
source: We searched S. mediterranea genomic and EST databases (Labbé et al., 2012; Robb et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015) for candidate ommochrome biosynthesis enzymes using a reciprocal BLAST approach (Materials and methods) and identified a total of 7 genes corresponding to the first 3 steps in the pathway (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis and data shown in Figure 2B and source data.

claim: Apparent absence of phenoxazinone synthetase in S. mediterranea is consistent with prior analyses of other animal genomes, including those of ommochrome-producing species.
source: Apparent absence of the terminal enzyme, phenoxazinone synthetase, is consistent with prior analyses of other animal genomes, including those of ommochrome-producing species (e.g., Croucher et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Croucher et al., 2013.

claim: Absence of phenoxazinone synthetase may reflect non-enzymatic oxidation of 3-hydroxykynurenine.
source: and may reflect non-enzymatic oxidation of 3-hydroxykynurenine (Wiley and Forrest, 1981).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wiley and Forrest, 1981 and represents a speculative explanation.

claim: Smed-kynurenine 3-monooxygenase-1 (KMO-1) exhibited pigment cell-specific or enriched expression.
source: Smed-kynurenine 3-monooxygenase-1 (KMO-1), 1 of 3 S. mediterranea KMO homologs, exhibited pigment cell-specific or enriched expression – staining was evident in cells distributed across the entire surface of the animal, but excluded from the unpigmented regions of the photoreceptors.
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nearly all KMO-1-expressing cells were lost during light-induced depigmentation.
source: Nearly all KMO-1-expressing cells were lost during light-induced depigmentation (see below).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: KMO-1 represents the first marker for a planarian pigment cell outside of the melanin-producing cells of the eye cups.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first marker for a planarian pigment cell outside of the melanin-producing cells of the eye cups (Lapan and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, supported by citation to Lapan and Reddien, 2011.

claim: Smed-kynurenine 3-monooxygenase-2 (KMO-2) appeared to be expressed in body pigment cells in addition to the gut.
source: The second KMO homolog, Smed-kynurenine 3-monooxygenase-2 (KMO-2), also appeared to be expressed in body pigment cells (in addition to the gut)
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: KMO-3 was expressed in a small group of cells of unknown function clustered anterior to the pharynx.
source: while the third, KMO-3, was expressed in a small group of cells of unknown function clustered anterior to the pharynx.
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Smed-tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO) was expressed in the gut.
source: Smed-tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO) was expressed in the gut.
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Smed-indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) exhibited an expression pattern resembling that of KMO-1.
source: Smed-indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) exhibited an expression pattern resembling that of KMO-1
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Smed-kynurenine formamidase-1 and -2 (KFM-1 and -2) showed specific or enriched expression in the central nervous system and/or gut.
source: The 2 remaining pathway genes, Smed-kynurenine formamidase-1 and -2 (KFM-1 and -2), showed specific or enriched expression in the central nervous system and/or gut.
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: KMO-1(RNAi) animals developed a yellow hue.
source: KMO-1(RNAi) animals developed a yellow hue.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: KMO-3(RNAi) animals developed a yellow hue.
source: This phenotype was also evident in KMO-3(RNAi) animals
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of all 3 KMO homologs did not alter the yellow color change.
source: simultaneous knockdown of all 3 KMO homologs did not alter the color change.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RNAi knockdown of TDO resulted in a charcoal grey color that was particularly apparent in the regeneration blastema.
source: RNAi knockdown of TDO resulted in a charcoal grey color that was particularly apparent in the regeneration blastema, the mass of stem cell-derived tissue that forms at sites of amputation (Figure 2D, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with a pharmacological TDO inhibitor phenocopied the TDO(RNAi) effect.
source: Treatment with a pharmacological TDO inhibitor phenocopied the TDO(RNAi) effect (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At most a subtle color change was detected in IDO(RNAi) animals.
source: Although IDO catalyzes the same reaction as TDO, we detected at most a subtle color change in IDO(RNAi) animals
evidence: This is an observational result from RNAi experiments.

claim: No enhanced phenotype was observed following double knockdown of IDO and TDO.
source: and did not observe an enhanced phenotype following double knockdown.
evidence: This is an observational result from RNAi experiments.

claim: No RNAi phenotypes were apparent for the 2 KFM homologs when targeted individually or in combination.
source: No RNAi phenotypes were apparent for the 2 KFM homologs when targeted individually or in combination.
evidence: This is an observational result from RNAi experiments.

claim: The RNAi results are consistent with the prior identification of TDO (vermilion) and KMO (cinnabar), but not KFM eye color mutants in Drosophila.
source: These results are consistent with the prior identification of TDO (vermilion) and KMO (cinnabar), but not KFM eye color mutants in Drosophila (Searles and Voelker, 1986; Warren et al., 1996)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Searles and Voelker, 1986 and Warren et al., 1996.

claim: The RNAi results are consistent with the potential for non-enzymatic generation of kynurenine from formylkynurenine.
source: as well as the potential for non-enzymatic generation of kynurenine from formylkynurenine (Linzen, 1974).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Linzen, 1974.

claim: Fixed G. dorotocephala showed intense red fluorescence at 400–440 nm excitation.
source: We reproduced previous results showing intense red fluorescence in fixed G. dorotocephala at 400–440 nm excitation (MacRae, 1961)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to MacRae, 1961.

claim: D. japonica was highly fluorescent under 400–440 nm excitation.
source: and found the related species Dugesia japonica was also highly fluorescent under these conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S. mediterranea exhibited minimal fluorescence compared to G. dorotocephala and D. japonica.
source: S. mediterranea exhibited minimal fluorescence by comparison
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: KMO-1(RNAi) S. mediterranea animals showed a dramatic increase in fluorescence relative to negative controls.
source: however, KMO-1(RNAi) animals showed a dramatic increase in fluorescence relative to negative controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: KMO-1(RNAi) extracts demonstrated bright red fluorescence under black light.
source: Like G. dorotocephala and D. japonica extracts, KMO-1(RNAi) extracts demonstrated bright red fluorescence under black light (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: KMO-1(RNAi) extracts demonstrated a characteristic porphyrin absorption spectrum with a sharp peak (the 'Soret' band) around 400 nm.
source: as well as a characteristic porphyrin absorption spectrum (Huang et al., 2000) with a sharp peak (the 'Soret' band) around 400 nm (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by absorption spectra data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Huang et al., 2000.

claim: Faint fluorescence and a very small, yet reproducible Soret peak were apparent for S. mediterranea controls.
source: Importantly, faint fluorescence and a very small, yet reproducible Soret peak were apparent for S. mediterranea controls.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence and absorption spectra data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: S. mediterranea makes porphyrins like G. dorotocephala, but at substantially lower levels, or primarily in a non-fluorescent form.
source: We conclude that S. mediterranea makes porphyrins like G. dorotocephala, but at substantially lower levels, or primarily in a non-fluorescent (e.g., reduced or metal-chelate) form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fluorescence and absorption spectra data.

claim: The effects of KMO-1 knockdown suggest that porphyrin biosynthesis occurs in pigment cells and may be suppressed by ommochromes.
source: The effects of KMO-1 knockdown further suggest that porphyrin biosynthesis occurs in pigment cells and may be suppressed by ommochromes (Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the KMO-1 RNAi results showing increased porphyrin fluorescence.

claim: S. mediterranea homologs of ALAS, ALA dehydratase (ALAD), and PBG deaminase (PBGD) were highly expressed in pigment cells.
source: Strikingly, S. mediterranea homologs of ALAS, ALA dehydratase (ALAD), and PBG deaminase (PBGD), enzymes catalyzing the first 3 reactions in metazoan heme biosynthesis, were highly expressed in pigment cells
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 5 remaining genes in the heme biosynthesis pathway were expressed predominantly or exclusively in cell types other than pigment cells.
source: while the 5 remaining genes in the pathway were expressed predominantly or exclusively in other cell types (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PBGD-1-expressing cells were located just beneath the epithelium.
source: In agreement with histological analyses of Dugesia gonocephala chromatophores (Palladini et al., 1979), PBGD-1-expressing cells were located just beneath the epithelium (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by tissue section data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Palladini et al., 1979.

claim: PBGD-1-expressing cells exhibited a dendritic morphology characteristic of other pigment-producing cell types.
source: and exhibited a dendritic morphology also characteristic of other pigment-producing cell types (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Smed-PBGD-1 (PBGD-1) was co-expressed with KMO-1.
source: Double fluorescent in situ hybridization (dFISH) confirmed Smed-PBGD-1 (PBGD-1) was co-expressed with KMO-1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Over 90% of KMO-1-positive cells were co-labeled with PBGD-1 and vice versa.
source: Over 90% of KMO-1-positive cells were co-labeled with PBGD-1 and vice versa (n = 11 animals analyzed by confocal microscopy).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from double FISH analysis.

claim: ALAS(RNAi) animals became lighter than negative controls prior to dying.
source: Specifically, while ALAS(RNAi) animals developed morphological defects culminating in 100% lethality, they became lighter than negative controls prior to dying (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PBGD-1(RNAi) animals were viable and showed a more pronounced reduction in pigmentation.
source: PBGD-1(RNAi) animals were viable and showed a more pronounced reduction in pigmentation (Figure 4F, top)
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PBGD-1(RNAi) animals eventually turned completely white with sustained RNAi feeding.
source: eventually turning completely white with sustained RNAi feeding (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: PBGD-1(RNAi) animals failed to produce new body pigment in the blastema following amputation.
source: Following amputation, PBGD-1(RNAi) animals failed to produce new body pigment in the blastema (Figure 4F, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ALAD-1 knockdown disrupted pigment biosynthesis in newly regenerated tissue.
source: ALAD-1 knockdown, while not effecting a pigmentation change in uncut animals, also disrupted pigment biosynthesis in newly regenerated tissue.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No changes in pigmentation were evident in intact or regenerating animals following knockdown of the remaining heme biosynthesis enzymes.
source: No changes in pigmentation were evident in either intact or regenerating animals following knockdown of the remaining heme biosynthesis enzymes
evidence: This is an observational result from RNAi experiments.

claim: RNAi phenotypes unrelated to pigmentation and 100% lethality were observed for PBGD-4 and Smed-uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase-1 (UROD-1).
source: though RNAi phenotypes unrelated to pigmentation and 100% lethality were observed for PBGD-4 and Smed-uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase-1 (UROD-1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi phenotype data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The first 3 enzymes in heme biosynthesis are expressed in the body pigment cells of S. mediterranea and are required for pigmentation.
source: To summarize, we found the first 3 enzymes in heme biosynthesis are expressed in the body pigment cells of S. mediterranea and are required for pigmentation
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the gene expression and RNAi data.

claim: UROS and the remaining enzymes in the heme biosynthesis pathway are not expressed (or are limiting) in S. mediterranea pigment cells, and are dispensable for pigment biosynthesis.
source: while UROS and the remaining enzymes in the pathway are not expressed (or are limiting) in this cell type, and are dispensable for pigment biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the gene expression and RNAi data.

claim: S. mediterranea pigment cells share a metabolic bottleneck with the erythroid cells of individuals suffering from congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP).
source: These results imply that S. mediterranea pigment cells share a metabolic bottleneck with the erythroid cells of individuals suffering from the rare, autosomal recessive disorder congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP) (Xu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and supported by a citation to Xu et al., 1996.

claim: Patients with CEP have reduction-of-function mutations in uroporphyrinogen III synthase (UROS).
source: Patients with this condition, also known as Gunther's disease, have reduction-of-function mutations in uroporphyrinogen III synthase (UROS), the 4th enzyme in heme biosynthesis
evidence: This is a statement about CEP based on established medical knowledge.

claim: CEP patients produce high levels of porphyrins in their erythroid cells.
source: and consequently produce high levels of porphyrins in their erythroid cells (Discussion).
evidence: This is a statement about CEP based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Some of the porphyrin molecules generated by CEP patients accumulate in the skin, causing severe cutaneous photosensitivity usually beginning in infancy.
source: Some of the porphyrin molecules generated by CEP patients accumulate in the skin, causing severe cutaneous photosensitivity usually beginning in infancy (Xu et al., 1996; Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Karim et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xu et al., 1996, Balwani and Desnick, 2012, and Karim et al., 2015.

claim: Red light (625 nm) was sufficient to induce full bodily depigmentation in S. mediterranea.
source: Consistent with a porphyrin-based mechanism, red light (625 nm) was sufficient to induce full bodily depigmentation (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The antioxidants dimethylthiourea (DMTU) and ascorbic acid exerted inhibitory effects on light-induced depigmentation.
source: while the antioxidants dimethylthiourea (DMTU) and ascorbic acid exerted inhibitory effects (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hypoxia was protective against light-induced depigmentation.
source: Hypoxia was also protective (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depigmentation was due to pigment cell loss.
source: We further determined that depigmentation was due to pigment cell loss – light exposure eliminated KMO-1/PBGD-1-positive cells, with no apparent decrease in expression of these genes within remaining pigment cells at intermediate timepoints (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both white light and red light induced a significant increase in cell death, as measured by whole-mount TUNEL.
source: Both white light and red light induced a significant increase in cell death, as measured by whole-mount TUNEL (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Systemic induction of cell death by RNAi knockdown of a BCL-2 homolog results in large tissue lesions and lysis.
source: Although we were unable to determine the cellular specificity of this response with existing methods, systemic induction of cell death by RNAi knockdown of a BCL-2 homolog results in large tissue lesions and lysis (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: Large tissue lesions and lysis were rarely observed following white light exposure and never observed with red light.
source: These phenotypes were rarely observed following white light exposure and never observed with red light, suggesting cell death is not systemically induced in these contexts.
evidence: This is an observational result from light exposure experiments.

claim: KMO-1(RNAi) animals showed increased photosensitivity, with 100% failing to survive 48 hr of light exposure.
source: As predicted, KMO-1(RNAi) animals showed increased photosensitivity, with 100% failing to survive 48 hr of light exposure, less than 1/3 the exposure time used to achieve depigmentation in controls.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNAi and light exposure experiments.

claim: Simultaneous PBGD-1 knockdown fully rescued viability of KMO-1(RNAi) animals exposed to light.
source: Simultaneous PBGD-1 (but not FECH-1) knockdown fully rescued viability (n = 20 animals per condition analyzed in 2 independent experiments).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from double RNAi and light exposure experiments.

claim: PBGD-1 is required for porphyrin biosynthesis in pigment cells.
source: We conclude that PBGD-1 is required for porphyrin biosynthesis in pigment cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments showing that PBGD-1 knockdown suppresses porphyrin fluorescence and photosensitivity.

claim: PBGD-1 knockdown suppressed light-induced depigmentation.
source: However, we did observe partial protection from light-induced depigmentation when PBGD-1(RNAi) animals were light exposed prior to developing full phenotypic expressivity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PBGD-1 knockdown conferred protection from light-induced pigment cell loss.
source: Furthermore, by using a KMO-1 riboprobe to label pigment cells by in situ hybridization, we showed PBGD-1 knockdown conferred protection from light-induced pigment cell loss (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Light-induced depigmentation in S. mediterranea is due to the photosensitizing action of porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells.
source: We conclude that light-induced depigmentation in S. mediterranea is due to the photosensitizing action of porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing porphyrin production, light-induced cell death, and rescue by PBGD-1 knockdown.

claim: Planarians can survive for months without feeding, undergoing an up to ~20-fold reduction in size through a tissue remodeling process involving increased cell death and decreased production of stem cell division progeny.
source: Planarians can survive for months without feeding, undergoing an up to ~20-fold reduction in size through a tissue remodeling process involving increased cell death and decreased production of stem cell division progeny (Pellettieri et al., 2010; González-Estévez et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pellettieri et al., 2010 and González-Estévez et al., 2012.

claim: There is a correlation between how long animals were fasted prior to light exposure and the extent of photosensitivity.
source: During the course of this research, we noticed a correlation between how long animals were fasted prior to light exposure and the extent of photosensitivity.
evidence: This is an observational finding that led to further experiments.

claim: Depigmentation was strongly accelerated with starvation.
source: Depigmentation was strongly accelerated with starvation (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Starvation-induced photosensitivity was reversed by a single feeding 24 hr prior to initiation of light exposure.
source: and reversed by a single feeding 24 hr prior to initiation of light exposure (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No difference in TUNEL staining was evident between 7 and 14 day-starved animals exposed to a sublethal dose of gamma irradiation.
source: However, no difference in TUNEL staining was evident between 7 and 14 day-starved animals exposed to a sublethal dose of gamma irradiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduced nutrient intake induces hepatic ALAS expression in mammals through the cAMP/CREB/PGC-1α pathway.
source: Reduced nutrient intake induces hepatic ALAS expression in mammals through the cAMP/CREB/PGC- 1α pathway (Handschin et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Handschin et al., 2005.

claim: When hepatic ALAS induction occurs in the presence of a heme biosynthesis bottleneck, as in acute porphyria patients, it can result in porphyrin accumulation.
source: When this occurs in the presence of a heme biosynthesis bottleneck, as in acute porphyria patients, it can result in porphyrin accumulation.
evidence: This is an explanation of disease mechanism based on established understanding of acute porphyrias.

claim: ALAS expression was elevated by starvation in S. mediterranea.
source: We found that ALAS expression was likewise elevated by starvation in S. mediterranea (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Fasting leads to increased porphyrin levels in D. japonica tissue homogenates.
source: and took advantage of the strong porphyrin fluorescence in D. japonica (Figure 3A,C) to show that fasting also leads to increased porphyrin levels in tissue homogenates (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Egg yolk was slightly less effective than liver in reversing starvation-induced photosensitivity.
source: Egg yolk (another laboratory food source) was slightly less effective than liver in reversing starvation-induced photosensitivity (Figure 7E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Addition of exogenous heme had no impact on starvation-induced photosensitivity.
source: However, addition of exogenous heme had no impact.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Porphyrin levels in planarians are at least partly influenced by metabolic regulation of ALAS expression, as in acute porphyrias.
source: While our results do not exclude a role for dietary heme in regulation of porphyrin biosynthesis in planarians, they do suggest porphyrin levels are at least partly influenced by metabolic regulation of ALAS expression, as in acute porphyrias.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing ALAS upregulation with starvation and the effects of different food sources.

claim: S. mediterranea produces both ommochromes and porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells.
source: Our results indicate that S. mediterranea produces both ommochromes and porphyrins in its subepithelial pigment cells
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Prolonged light exposure eliminates S. mediterranea pigment cells through a mechanism involving porphyrin-dependent photosensitization.
source: and that prolonged light exposure eliminates these cells through a mechanism involving porphyrin-dependent photosensitization (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The black color of the eye cups in species including S. mediterranea, D. ryukyuensis, and likely G. dorotocephala is due to melanins.
source: The black color of the eye cups in species including S. mediterranea, D. ryukyuensis, and likely G. dorotocephala is due to melanins (Ness et al., 1996; Hase et al., 2006; Lapan and Reddien, 2011; Lambrus et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ness et al., 1996, Hase et al., 2006, Lapan and Reddien, 2011, and Lambrus et al., 2015.

claim: The brown body color in D. ryukyuensis has been attributed to ommochromes.
source: while the brown body color in D. ryukyuensis and G. dorotocephala has been attributed to ommochromes and porphyrins, respectively (MacRae, 1956; 1959; 1961; 1963; Hase et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hase et al., 2006.

claim: The brown body color in G. dorotocephala has been attributed to porphyrins.
source: while the brown body color in D. ryukyuensis and G. dorotocephala has been attributed to ommochromes and porphyrins, respectively (MacRae, 1956; 1959; 1961; 1963; Hase et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to MacRae, 1956; 1959; 1961; 1963.

claim: Hemoglobin has been identified in free-living and endosymbiotic rhabdocoels as well as trematode parasites.
source: Hemoglobin has been identified in free-living and endosymbiotic rhabdocoels as well as trematode parasites (Young and Harris, 1973; Phillips, 1978; Jennings and Cannon, 1987; Kiger et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Young and Harris, 1973, Phillips, 1978, Jennings and Cannon, 1987, and Kiger et al., 1998.

claim: The RNAi phenotypes of KMO-1 and PBGD-1 imply biochemical or genetic interactions between ommochromes and porphyrins or their underlying biosynthetic pathways.
source: The RNAi phenotypes of KMO-1 and PBGD-1 further imply biochemical or genetic interactions between ommochromes and porphyrins or their underlying biosynthetic pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi phenotypes showing that KMO-1 knockdown increases porphyrin fluorescence and PBGD-1 knockdown causes loss of all pigmentation.

claim: Light-exposed S. mediterranea repigment when returned to a dark environment, presumably through replacement of lost pigment cells.
source: Additionally, the observation that light-exposed S. mediterranea repigment when returned to a dark environment (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E), presumably through replacement of lost pigment cells (Figure 5C), sets the stage for mechanistic analyses of pigment cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E and Figure 5C, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Planarians have long attracted the interest of biologists investigating regeneration.
source: Planarians have long attracted the interest of biologists investigating regeneration (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002.

claim: Planarians have recently emerged as a useful invertebrate model for human disorders including Usher syndrome and cystic kidney disease.
source: and have recently emerged as a useful invertebrate model for human disorders including Usher syndrome (Lapan and Reddien, 2012) and cystic kidney disease (Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lapan and Reddien, 2012 and Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015.

claim: The porphyrias are classified based on whether intermediates in heme biosynthesis are formed predominantly in the liver or bone marrow.
source: The porphyrias are classified based on multiple criteria, including: 1) whether intermediates in heme biosynthesis are formed predominantly in the liver or bone marrow
evidence: This is a statement about the classification of porphyrias based on established medical knowledge.

claim: The porphyrias are classified based on whether symptoms manifest primarily as skin lesions or neurovisceral episodes.
source: 2) whether symptoms manifest primarily as skin lesions or neurovisceral episodes
evidence: This is a statement about the classification of porphyrias based on established medical knowledge.

claim: The porphyrias are classified based on the step at which heme biosynthesis is disrupted.
source: and 3) the step at which heme biosynthesis is disrupted.
evidence: This is a statement about the classification of porphyrias based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Light-induced depigmentation in planarians combines aspects of multiple porphyria disease variants.
source: Light-induced depigmentation in planarians combines aspects of multiple disease variants (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison with human porphyrias.

claim: UROS deficiency is the blockage in heme biosynthesis underlying CEP.
source: UROS deficiency, the blockage in heme biosynthesis underlying CEP, is also the apparent determinant of physiological porphyrin biosynthesis in S. mediterranea.
evidence: This is a statement about CEP based on established medical knowledge.

claim: In the absence of UROS, its linear tetrapyrrole substrate hydroxymethylbilane undergoes spontaneous cyclization to form uroporphyrinogen I.
source: In the absence of this enzyme, its linear tetrapyrrole substrate hydroxymethylbilane undergoes spontaneous cyclization to form uroporphyrinogen I, a pathogenic isomer of uroporphyrinogen III that can in turn undergo spontaneous oxidation to form porphyrins.
evidence: This describes the biochemical consequence of UROS deficiency based on established knowledge.

claim: Uroporphyrinogen I is a pathogenic isomer of uroporphyrinogen III that can undergo spontaneous oxidation to form porphyrins.
source: In the absence of this enzyme, its linear tetrapyrrole substrate hydroxymethylbilane undergoes spontaneous cyclization to form uroporphyrinogen I, a pathogenic isomer of uroporphyrinogen III that can in turn undergo spontaneous oxidation to form porphyrins.
evidence: This describes the biochemical properties of uroporphyrinogen I based on established knowledge.

claim: The episodic nature of acute porphyria symptoms is attributed to hepatic induction of ALAS1 by endogenous and exogenous factors including dieting or fasting.
source: The episodic nature of acute porphyria symptoms is attributed to hepatic induction of ALAS1, 1 of 2 human isoforms of the gene, by endogenous and exogenous factors including dieting or fasting (Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Karim et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Balwani and Desnick, 2012 and Karim et al., 2015.

claim: Dieting or fasting can pose a weight-loss challenge for individuals carrying acute porphyria disease alleles.
source: This can pose a weight-loss challenge for individuals carrying disease alleles
evidence: This is a clinical implication based on the relationship between fasting and acute porphyria attacks.

claim: Dieting or fasting may be a complicating factor in bariatric surgery for individuals with acute porphyrias.
source: and may be a complicating factor in bariatric surgery (Lopes et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lopes et al., 2008.

claim: In mice, fasting-induced ALAS upregulation is dependent on PGC-1α, and inhibited by insulin signaling.
source: In mice, fasting-induced ALAS upregulation is dependent on PGC- 1α, and inhibited by insulin signaling (Scassa et al., 2004; Handschin et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Scassa et al., 2004 and Handschin et al., 2005.

claim: Insulin-like signaling has been described in planarians.
source: While we have been unable to identify a PGC- 1α homolog in S. mediterranea, insulin-like signaling has been described (Miller and Newmark, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miller and Newmark, 2012.

claim: Existing animal models of acute porphyrias commonly rely on chemical treatments to evoke phenotypes resembling human disease symptoms.
source: Existing animal models of acute porphyrias commonly rely on chemical treatments to evoke phenotypes resembling human disease symptoms.
evidence: This is a statement about existing animal models based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The fluorescence of fixed planarian animals provides a convenient means of assessing porphyrin levels in vivo.
source: Third, the fluorescence of fixed animals and easily inducible depigmentation response provide a convenient means of assessing porphyrin levels and their photosensitizing activity in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the planarian model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The easily inducible depigmentation response in planarians provides a convenient means of assessing porphyrin photosensitizing activity in vivo.
source: Third, the fluorescence of fixed animals and easily inducible depigmentation response provide a convenient means of assessing porphyrin levels and their photosensitizing activity in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the planarian model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The protective effect of DMTU against light exposure constitutes proof of principle for drug screening in planarians.
source: The protective effect of DMTU against light exposure (Figure 5B) constitutes proof of principle for such an approach.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the planarian model based on the DMTU experiment.

claim: Porphyrias are usually manageable diseases.
source: Although porphyrias are usually manageable diseases
evidence: This is a general statement about porphyrias based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Reliance on intravenous heme or liver transplantation to treat severe porphyria cases can result in significant complications.
source: reliance on intravenous heme or liver transplantation to treat severe cases can result in significant complications (Seth et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Seth et al., 2007.

claim: There is no approved prophylactic treatment for patients who suffer recurrent acute porphyria attacks.
source: There is no approved prophylactic treatment for patients who suffer recurrent attacks.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of porphyria treatment based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Planarians represent an experimentally tractable animal model for exploring both physiological and pathological roles of porphyrins.
source: We suggest planarians represent an experimentally tractable animal model in which to explore both physiological and pathological roles of porphyrins, and to seek new avenues for modulating their biosynthesis toward therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the planarian model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Planarians represent an experimentally tractable animal model for seeking new avenues for modulating porphyrin biosynthesis toward therapeutic benefit.
source: We suggest planarians represent an experimentally tractable animal model in which to explore both physiological and pathological roles of porphyrins, and to seek new avenues for modulating their biosynthesis toward therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the planarian model based on the experimental findings.
